# What my grandmother's kitchen taught me about patience

My grandmother rolled her own noodles every Sunday, and for years I thought that was just a fact of
the world, like tides or gravity. It wasn't until I tried it myself, at twenty-six, standing in her
kitchen with flour up to my elbows, that I understood how much practice sits underneath something
that looks effortless.

She never measured anything. Flour went in until the dough "felt right," a phrase that meant nothing
to me the first dozen times she said it. I'd ask how much, and she'd shrug and add a little more
water, or a little more flour, correcting by feel in a way I couldn't replicate no matter how
closely I watched her hands.

I ruined four batches before I got one she'd actually serve to guests. The first was too wet and
stuck to everything. The second tore apart the moment it hit boiling water. By the third, I was
close, but the noodles came out uneven, thick in places and paper thin in others. She tasted the
fourth batch, chewed for a long moment, and finally nodded.

I asked her, half joking, if she was ever going to just write the recipe down. She laughed and said
some things are less recipe than habit, something you build with your hands until your hands remember them
without you. I think about that a lot now, whenever I'm learning something new and getting
frustrated that it isn't clicking yet. Some things really do just take four ruined batches first.
